cases.answer: In Saffire-II, sample 2-5, a 5 cm wide cotton-fiberglass sample, burned its full 29 cm at a flame spread rate of 2.1 mm/s. Sample 2-5 was tested in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at about 22.1% O2.

In the FLEX report, the burning rate is defined as the average burning rate constant from a linear fit of the droplet diameter squared versus time, taken from shortly after ignition to extinction. Table IX reports the FLEX burning rate in mm2/s. The PSI-69 column header says 'mm'.

In Saffire-II combined PMMA and Nomex sample 2-7, tested in microgravity, the PMMA section burned (5 cm) but the adjoining Nomex did not burn. The Saffire-II data row for sample 2-7 reads "2-7 80 W 9.2 s 140 s 5 cm & 0 ii n/a (Nomex) ~ 0 (Nomex) n/a (Nomex)". The evidence gives "5 cm & 0" and "~ 0 (Nomex)" for the Nomex portion.

Early numerical and experimental evidence suggested Lunar gravity could be more hazardous because flame spread rate as a function of gravity peaks near Lunar gravity. Theoretical and experimental results have shown that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity such as Lunar-g.

In SoFIE imagery of 0.1-mm-thick PMMA, radiative quenching is shown when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s. In the same SoFIE imagery of 0.1-mm-thick PMMA, the flame is shown nearing blow off extinction as the flow velocity crosses 40 cm/s.

Saffire IV-VI found that the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide: "Overall, the temperature and pressure rise in the spacecraft were found to be less significant than the increase in carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide." Saffire experiments were designed to run in Orbital ATK's Cygnus vehicle after it unberthed from the International Space Station. The aim was to study how rapidly a large-scale fire grows in low gravity.

In 1997, a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister in Mir's Kvant-1 module ignited when it was activated, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke. The flame blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz. Investigators identified latex working glove material inadvertently introduced into the canister as the most likely cause of the fire. The crew quickly donned oxygen masks, and Korzun began dousing the flame with foam from a fire extinguisher.
Saffire-II sample 2-6 was a cotton-fiberglass sample tested in microgravity. It burned its full length at 2.6 mm/s. The tabulated values are "2-6 80 W 9.2 s 115 s 29 cm 2.6 mm/s".
